Here $\lambda(15)=\lcm(2,4)=4$ and $\lambda(35)=\lcm(4,6)=12$; the first $1$ occurs at
$k=\lambda$ in both cases, in accordance with Theorem~\ref{thm:legible}.

\section{Factor recovery: a false formula and its repair}

Suppose an oracle supplies $\lambda(N)$. A recurring informal claim is that one may set
$p+q=N-\lambda(N)+1$ and solve $X^2-(p+q)X+N$. The reasoning appeals to
$\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)=N-(p+q)+1$ and then silently replaces $\varphi(N)$ by $\lambda(N)$.
This is invalid.

\begin{theorem}[The naive recovery formula is false]\label{thm:false}
Take $p=5$, $q=13$, so $N=65$. Then $\lambda(N)=\lcm(4,12)=12$ and
\[
N-\lambda(N)+1 = 65-12+1 = 54 \;\ne\; 18 = p+q .
\]
\end{theorem}

The discrepancy is exactly $\gcd(p-1,q-1)=\gcd(4,12)=4$.

\begin{theorem}[Corrected recovery identity]\label{thm:repair}
For all integers $p,q\ge1$, with $\lambda=\lcm(p-1,q-1)$,
\[
\gcd(p-1,q-1)\cdot\lambda \;+\; (p+q) \;=\; pq+1 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\gcd(m,n)\lcm(m,n)=mn$ with $m=p-1$, $n=q-1$ turns the first term into $(p-1)(q-1)$.
Writing $p=a+1$, $q=b+1$, the claim becomes the polynomial identity
$ab+(a+1)+(b+1)=(a+1)(b+1)+1$.
\end{proof}

Equivalently $\varphi(N)+(p+q)=N+1$ with $\varphi(N)=\gcd(p-1,q-1)\cdot\lambda(N)$. The
period gives $\lambda$, not $\varphi$; the missing datum is $\gcd(p-1,q-1)$.

\begin{corollary}[Recovery under a coprimality guard]\label{cor:guard}
If $\gcd(p-1,q-1)=1$ then $\lambda(N)+(p+q)=N+1$: the naive formula is correct exactly in
this case.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Vieta uniqueness]\label{lem:vieta}
Let $s,N\ge0$ and suppose $a+b=s=a'+b'$ and $ab=N=a'b'$ with $a\le b$, $a'\le b'$ in
$\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$. Then $a=a'$ and $b=b'$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both $a,a'$ satisfy $X(s-X)=N$, so $(a-a')(a+a'-s)=0$ over $\mathbb Z$. In the first case
$a=a'$ and hence $b=b'$. In the second, $a'=s-a=b$ and $b'=a$; with $a\le b$, $a'\le b'$
this forces $a=b$, so again $a=a'$, $b=b'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Full recovery from the period]\label{thm:recover}
Let $N=pq$ with $p<q$ distinct primes satisfying $\gcd(p-1,q-1)=1$, and let
$\lambda=\lambda(N)$ be the least period. If $a\le b$ are non-negative integers with
$ab=N$ and $a+b=N+1-\lambda$, then $a=p$ and $b=q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Corollary~\ref{cor:guard}, $N+1-\lambda=p+q$. So $(a,b)$ and $(p,q)$ share sum and
product and are both ordered; Lemma~\ref{lem:vieta} identifies them.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:guard}
The guard is restrictive. If $p$ and $q$ are both odd then $2$ divides both $p-1$ and
$q-1$, so $\gcd(p-1,q-1)\ge2$ and the guard \emph{fails}; it holds only when one prime is
$2$. Consequently the naive formula is wrong in every case of practical interest, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:repair} is not a pedantic footnote but the substantive statement.
\end{remark}

\section{Squarefree moduli and the Korselt bridge}\label{sec:sqfree}

Nothing above used the number of prime factors of $N$.

\begin{theorem}[Squarefree divisibility criterion]\label{thm:sqfree}
Let $N$ be squarefree, $p$ a prime with $p\mid N$, and $k\ge1$. Then
$p\mid F_N(k) \iff (p-1)\nmid k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $N=pm$; squarefreeness gives $p\nmid m$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:divis}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[General Carmichael periodicity]\label{thm:gencar}
For squarefree $N\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\gcd\bigl(F_N(k),N\bigr)=1 \iff \lambda(N)\mid k$,
where $\lambda(N)=\lcm_{p\mid N}(p-1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The gcd is $\ne1$ iff some prime $p\mid N$ divides $F_N(k)$, iff by
Theorem~\ref{thm:sqfree} some $p\mid N$ has $(p-1)\nmid k$. Negating gives $(p-1)\mid k$
for all $p\mid N$, i.e.\ $\lambda(N)\mid k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Fermat/Giuga direction]\label{prop:giuga}
For a prime $p$, $\sum_{a=1}^{p} a^{\,p-1}\equiv-1 \pmod p$, so $\gcd(F_p(p-1),p)=1$: a
prime is never revealed by itself.
\end{proposition}

Recall \emph{Korselt's criterion}: a composite squarefree $N$ is a Carmichael number if and
only if $(p-1)\mid(N-1)$ for every prime $p\mid N$.

\begin{theorem}[Korselt bridge]\label{thm:korselt}
Let $N\ge2$ be squarefree. Then
\[
\bigl(\forall p\mid N \text{ prime},\ (p-1)\mid(N-1)\bigr)
\iff \gcd\bigl(F_N(N-1),\,N\bigr)=1 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:gencar} at $k=N-1$: coprimality is $\lambda(N)\mid N-1$, which
unfolds by the definition of lcm into the Korselt conditions.
\end{proof}

Thus \emph{Carmichael numbers are exactly the squarefree moduli on which the power-sum
reveal at the natural exponent $k=N-1$ is completely uninformative}. The same divisibility
that makes them fool the Fermat primality test makes them defeat this method there.

\begin{example}
$N=561=3\cdot11\cdot17$, the smallest Carmichael number: $\lambda(561)=\lcm(2,10,16)=80$
and $80\mid560$, so $\gcd(F_{561}(560),561)=1$. The failure is exponent-specific: exponents
that are not multiples of $80$ still leak information.
\end{example}

\section{Odd prime powers: lifting the exponent}\label{sec:primepow}

Squarefreeness was used exactly once, to ensure $p\nmid m$. We now remove it at odd primes.
The naive guess is that the governing condition at $p^e$ is $\lambda(p^e)=p^{e-1}(p-1)$.
It is not: for $p^e=9$ one computes $\sum_{a<9}a^k\equiv6\equiv-3\pmod9$ for \emph{every
even} $k$, not merely for $k$ divisible by $\lambda(9)=6$. The $p$-part of the unit group
is invisible to the power sum.

\begin{lemma}[Block decomposition]\label{lem:block}
For $M,t\ge0$ and $f$ valued in an abelian group,
$\sum_{a=0}^{Mt-1} f(a)=\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\sum_{r=0}^{M-1} f(Mj+r)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Binomial with nilpotent increment]\label{lem:binom}
In a commutative ring, if $y^2=0$ then $(x+y)^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+(k+1)x^{k}y$ for all $k\ge0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Lift-the-exponent step]\label{thm:lte}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $e\ge2$, $k\ge1$. Then in $\Zmod{p^{e}}$,
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p^{e}-1} a^{k} \;=\; p\cdot\sum_{r=0}^{p^{e-1}-1} r^{k}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $M=p^{e-1}$ and write $a=Mj+r$ with $j<p$, $r<M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:block}). Modulo $p^e$
we have $M^2=0$ and $Mp=0$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:binom} with $x=r$, $y=Mj$, legitimate
since $(Mj)^2=M^2j^2=0$, obtaining $(Mj+r)^k=r^k+k\,r^{k-1}Mj$. Summing over $r$ and $j$,
the first part contributes $p\sum_{r<M}r^k$; the second carries the factor
$M\sum_{j<p}j=M\cdot p(p-1)/2$, and $p(p-1)/2$ is an integer multiple of $p$ precisely
\emph{because $p$ is odd}, so that part is a multiple of $Mp\equiv0$ and vanishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Prime-power Fermat sum]\label{thm:ppfermat}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $e\ge1$, $k\ge1$. Then
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p^{e}-1} a^{k} \;\equiv\;
\begin{cases} -\,p^{\,e-1} \pmod{p^{e}}, & (p-1)\mid k,\\[2pt]
\phantom{-}0 \pmod{p^{e}}, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $e$. Base $e=1$: Lemma~\ref{lem:fermat}, with $p^0=1$. Step:
Theorem~\ref{thm:lte} gives $\sum_{a<p^{e+1}}a^k\equiv p\sum_{a<p^{e}}a^k\pmod{p^{e+1}}$,
and multiplying the induction hypothesis (a congruence mod $p^e$) by $p$ yields a
congruence mod $p^{e+1}$; the value transforms as $p\cdot(-p^{e-1})=-p^{e}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Prime-power master formula]\label{thm:ppmaster}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $e\ge1$, $k\ge1$, and $N=p^{e}m$ with $p\nmid m$. Then
\[
\gcd\bigl(F_N(k),\,p^{e}\bigr) =
\begin{cases} p^{\,e-1}, & (p-1)\mid k,\\ p^{e}, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By the reduction of Proposition~\ref{prop:reduce} in $\Zmod{p^e}$ and
Theorem~\ref{thm:ppfermat}, $F_N(k)\equiv -m\,p^{e-1}$ or $0$ modulo $p^e$. In the second
case $p^e\mid F_N(k)$. In the first, $p^{e-1}$ divides $F_N(k)$ but $p^e$ does not, since
that would force $p\mid m$. Every divisor of $p^e$ is a power of $p$, so the gcd is
$p^{e-1}$ exactly.
\end{proof}

So a prime power $p^{e}\,\|\,N$ is revealed in full unless $(p-1)\mid k$, in which case
exactly one power of $p$ is lost.

\begin{example}
$N=45=3^2\cdot5$, $k=2$. Since $(3-1)\mid2$ the $3$-part drops from $9$ to $3$, while
$(5-1)\nmid2$ leaves the $5$-part full: $\gcd(F_{45}(2),45)=15$, as computation confirms.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[The prime $2$]
The prime $2$ is genuinely exceptional: the Gauss-sum step in Theorem~\ref{thm:lte} needs
$p$ odd. For $N=8$, and $k\ge2$, the gcd is $4$ for even $k$ and $8$ for odd $k$.
Determining the $2$-part of $\gcd(F_N(k),N)$ for $2^{e}\|N$, and assembling the local
formulas by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, remains open.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms and complexity}\label{sec:complexity}

\subsection{The reveal algorithm}
\emph{Input:} a semiprime $N$. \emph{Output:} a proper factor.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $k=1,2,3,\dots$:
\item \quad $S \leftarrow \sum_{a=1}^{N} a^{k} \bmod N$.
\item \quad $d \leftarrow \gcd(S,N)$.
\item \quad If $1<d<N$, return $d$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Correctness.} The loop terminates at $k^\ast=\min(p-1,q-1)$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:firsthit}, returning the larger prime.
\emph{Cost.} Each evaluation of $F_N(k)\bmod N$ costs $O(N)$ modular operations, and
$k^\ast\approx\sqrt N$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt}, so the total is $O(N^{3/2})$. Trial
division costs $O(\sqrt N)$ and Pollard's rho $O(N^{1/4})$: \emph{the power-sum method is
asymptotically worse than trial division.}

\subsection{The period-reading algorithm}
\emph{Input:} a semiprime $N$ with $\gcd(p-1,q-1)=1$. \emph{Output:} $\{p,q\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $k=1,2,\dots$: $g\leftarrow\gcd(F_N(k)\bmod N,\,N)$.
\item \quad If $g=1$: set $\lambda\leftarrow k$ and break.
\item $s\leftarrow N+1-\lambda$.
\item Solve $X^2-sX+N=0$ over $\mathbb Z$ and return the roots.
\end{enumerate}
Step~2 is Theorem~\ref{thm:legible}, Step~3 is Corollary~\ref{cor:guard}, and uniqueness of
the roots is Theorem~\ref{thm:recover}. Without the guard, Step~3 is invalid
(Theorem~\ref{thm:false}). Since $\lambda(N)$ can be $\Theta(N)$, the cost is $O(N^2)$.

\subsection{The period-finding barrier}
Both algorithms bottleneck on locating a distinguished exponent in a sequence of period
$\lambda(N)$, sampled one expensive point at a time; Theorem~\ref{thm:density} quantifies
the sparsity of informative points. This is the architecture that Shor's algorithm
dissolves: it extracts the period of $x\mapsto a^{x}\bmod N$ in polynomial time and
converts it to a factorization. Here we have a different sequence,
$k\mapsto\gcd(F_N(k),N)$, with the same signature --- an explicit function of $k$ whose
least period is $\lambda(N)$ and whose period determines the factorization (under the guard
of Theorem~\ref{thm:recover}, or with the correction of Theorem~\ref{thm:repair} in
general). The setting isolates exactly which step is hard.

\section{Numerical verification}

All eight agree with Corollary~\ref{cor:uncond}. Further checks: the period tables of
$g_{15}$ and $g_{35}$ above; the density count $\{4,6,8\}$ for $N=35$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:density}); $\gcd(6^4-1,35)=35$ versus $g_{35}(4)=7$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:robust}); $\gcd(F_{561}(560),561)=1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:korselt});
$\gcd(F_{45}(2),45)=15$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:ppmaster}); and for $p=5$, $q=13$,
$65-12+1=54\ne18$ while $\gcd(4,12)\cdot12+18=66=65+1$ (Theorems~\ref{thm:false},
\ref{thm:repair}).

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What the master formula buys}
The distinguishing feature of Theorem~\ref{thm:master} is \emph{completeness}. Pollard's
$p-1$ admits a success criterion but no closed form for its output; here every value is
determined, and the behaviour of $g_N$ reduces to two Boolean predicates. That is what makes
the exact least period, exact first-hit index, exact density count and exact Korselt
equivalence possible. Nothing in the downstream sections is an estimate.

\subsection{The correction matters}
By Remark~\ref{rem:guard}, for $N$ a product of two odd primes the guard
$\gcd(p-1,q-1)=1$ always fails. The naive recovery formula is therefore wrong in every case
of practical interest, and Theorem~\ref{thm:repair} identifies the missing datum as
$\gcd(p-1,q-1)$, which is not readable from the period. This narrows the gap between
``know the period'' and ``know the factorization'' to exactly one additional invariant.

\subsection{Carmichael numbers, twice}
Carmichael numbers appear in two roles: as \emph{moduli} on which $k=N-1$ is blind
(Theorem~\ref{thm:korselt}), and through the \emph{function} $\lambda$ as the least period
(Theorem~\ref{thm:legible}). This is no accident: both are the assertion
$\lambda(N)\mid k$, once at the specific $k=N-1$ and once as a general divisibility.

\subsection{The prime-power surprise}
The condition in Theorem~\ref{thm:ppfermat} is $(p-1)\mid k$, not $\lambda(p^e)\mid k$. The
mechanism is clean: the lift-the-exponent recursion multiplies the sum by $p$ at each level
without touching the $k$-dependence, so the base-case condition propagates unchanged. The
Gauss sum $\sum_{j<p}j=p(p-1)/2$ is the pivot, and its divisibility by $p$ is exactly the
oddness hypothesis.

\subsection{Relation to the quantum picture}
This is a classical structure theorem, not a quantum algorithm; but the shape is
instructive. The factorization of $N$ is not concealed in $g_N$ --- it is \emph{displayed},
the prime factors appearing literally as values. The barrier is the $O(N)$ sampling cost
combined with the sparsity of informative points. Both are exactly the obstacles a
period-finding subroutine removes.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{problem}[The prime $2$ and a global master formula]
Determine the $2$-part of $\gcd(F_N(k),N)$ for $2^{e}\|N$, and combine it with
Theorem~\ref{thm:ppmaster} via the Chinese Remainder Theorem to obtain a master formula
valid for arbitrary $N$. For $N=8$, and $k\ge2$, the gcd is $4$ for even $k$ and $8$ for odd $k$, so the
answer is not a direct analogue of the odd case.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Giuga's conjecture in power-sum form]
Giuga's conjecture asserts that no composite $n$ satisfies
$\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}a^{\,n-1}\equiv-1\pmod n$, while every prime does
(Proposition~\ref{prop:giuga}). Determine exactly which squarefree $n$ satisfy the local
conditions arising from Theorem~\ref{thm:sqfree}, and use Theorem~\ref{thm:ppmaster} to
rule out non-squarefree $n$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Sharper density statistics]
Average the exact count of Theorem~\ref{thm:density} over semiprimes $N\le X$, using the
distribution of $\gcd(p-1,q-1)$ and $\lcm(p-1,q-1)$, to obtain the expected proportion of
revealing exponents and hence the expected cost of a randomized exponent search.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Twisted power sums]
For a Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $N$, determine
$\gcd\bigl(\sum_{a=1}^{N}\chi(a)a^{k},\,N\bigr)$, and ask whether a nontrivial twist can
shift revealing exponents below $k^\ast=\min(p-1,q-1)$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Fast evaluation of $F_N(k)$]
The $O(N)$ per-evaluation cost dominates. $\sum_{a=1}^{N}a^k$ is a Faulhaber polynomial in
$N$ of degree $k+1$, computable in $O(k)$ operations given Bernoulli numbers, but
$k\approx\sqrt N$ and Bernoulli numbers modulo $N$ carry von Staudt--Clausen denominator
difficulties. Determine whether $F_N(k)\bmod N$ can be evaluated in $\mathrm{polylog}(N)$
time for $k\approx\sqrt N$, which would bring the reveal algorithm to $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$.
\end{problem}

\section{Conclusion}

We have given a complete closed-form description of $k\mapsto\gcd(\sum_{a=1}^{N}a^{k},N)$
for semiprime, squarefree and odd-prime-power moduli. The description determines every
value, the least period (the Carmichael function $\lambda(N)$), the exact first nontrivial
index $\min(p-1,q-1)<\sqrt N$, the exact count of informative exponents per period, and the
exact class of moduli on which $k=N-1$ is uninformative (the Carmichael numbers). Along the
way we correct a false factor-recovery formula and supply the identity that replaces it. As
a factoring procedure the method costs $O(N^{3/2})$ and is beaten by trial division; as
mathematics, it exhibits an integer sequence in which the factorization of $N$ is fully and
explicitly encoded --- in its values and in its period --- thereby isolating period finding
as the sole locus of difficulty.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core arithmetic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def lcm(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Least common multiple of two non-negative integers."""
    if a == 0 or b == 0:
        return 0
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b


def lcm_all(values: Iterable[int]) -> int:
    """Least common multiple of a finite family of positive integers."""
    result = 1
    for v in values:
        result = lcm(result, v)
    return result


def power_sum_mod(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """F_N(k) mod N  =  (1^k + 2^k + ... + N^k) mod N.

    Cost: O(N) modular exponentiations, which is the dominant cost of the
    whole method and the reason it is asymptotically worse than trial
    division.
    """
    total = 0
    for a in range(1, n + 1):
        total += pow(a, k, n)
    return total % n


def power_sum_gcd(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """g_N(k) = gcd(F_N(k), N)."""
    return gcd(power_sum_mod(n, k), n)


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Deterministic trial-division primality test (adequate at these sizes)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of n >= 1 as an exponent dictionary."""
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    m = n
    d = 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            m //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if m > 1:
        factors[m] = factors.get(m, 0) + 1
    return factors


def carmichael_squarefree(n: int) -> int:
    """lambda(N) = lcm over primes p | N of (p-1); valid for squarefree N."""
    return lcm_all(p - 1 for p in factorize(n))

    left = 1 if k % (p - 1) == 0 else p

def pollard_gcd(n: int, a: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Pollard p-1 style gcd:  gcd(a^M - 1, N)."""

    return n if r == 0 else r

def recover_factors_from_period(n: int, lam: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Recover {p,q} from N and lambda(N), valid when gcd(p-1,q-1) = 1.

    Solves X^2 - sX + N = 0 with s = N + 1 - lambda; returns None if the
    discriminant is not a perfect square (which signals that the guard fails).
    """
    s = n + 1 - lam
    disc = s * s - 4 * n
    if disc < 0:
        return None
    r = isqrt(disc)
    if r * r != disc or (s - r) % 2 != 0:
        return None
    a, b = (s - r) // 2, (s + r) // 2
    if a * b != n or a < 1:
        return None
    return (a, b)

def power_sum_factor(n: int, max_k: Optional[int] = None) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Find a proper factor of N by scanning k = 1, 2, 3, ...

    Returns (k, d) where d is the first proper nontrivial divisor found, or
    None if none is found within the bound.  By the first-hit theorem the
    successful k is min(p-1, q-1) for a semiprime N = pq.
    """
    if max_k is None:

    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        d = power_sum_gcd(n, k)
        if 1 < d < n:
            return (k, d)
    return None

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core arithmetic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def lcm(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Least common multiple of two non-negative integers."""
    if a == 0 or b == 0:
        return 0
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b


def lcm_all(values: Iterable[int]) -> int:
    """Least common multiple of a finite family of positive integers."""
    result = 1
    for v in values:
        result = lcm(result, v)
    return result


def power_sum_mod(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """F_N(k) mod N  =  (1^k + 2^k + ... + N^k) mod N.

    Cost: O(N) modular exponentiations, which is the dominant cost of the
    whole method and the reason it is asymptotically worse than trial
    division.
    """
    total = 0
    for a in range(1, n + 1):
        total += pow(a, k, n)
    return total % n


def power_sum_gcd(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """g_N(k) = gcd(F_N(k), N)."""
    return gcd(power_sum_mod(n, k), n)


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Deterministic trial-division primality test (adequate at these sizes)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of n >= 1 as an exponent dictionary."""
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    m = n
    d = 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            m //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if m > 1:
        factors[m] = factors.get(m, 0) + 1
    return factors


def carmichael_squarefree(n: int) -> int:
    """lambda(N) = lcm over primes p | N of (p-1); valid for squarefree N."""
    return lcm_all(p - 1 for p in factorize(n))

def recover_factors_from_period(n: int, lam: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Recover {p,q} from N and lambda(N), valid when gcd(p-1,q-1) = 1.

    Solves X^2 - sX + N = 0 with s = N + 1 - lambda; returns None if the
    discriminant is not a perfect square (which signals that the guard fails).
    """
    s = n + 1 - lam
    disc = s * s - 4 * n
    if disc < 0:
        return None
    r = isqrt(disc)
    if r * r != disc or (s - r) % 2 != 0:
        return None
    a, b = (s - r) // 2, (s + r) // 2
    if a * b != n or a < 1:
        return None
    return (a, b)

    """g_{pq}(k) for k = 1..kmax, in O(kmax) total time (no power sums)."""
    return [(1 if k % (p - 1) == 0 else p) * (1 if k % (q - 1) == 0 else q)

    lam = lcm(p - 1, q - 1)

    """lambda/(p-1) + lambda/(q-1) - 2, the exact census per period."""
    lam = lcm(p - 1, q - 1)

    """gcd(F_N(k), p^e) for an odd prime p with p^e || N.

Panel B — the density of revealing exponents.  Within one Carmichael period
lambda(N) = lcm(p-1,q-1), the number of exponents that expose a proper factor
is exactly
        lambda/(p-1) + lambda/(q-1) - 2 .
We plot the resulting *fraction* of a period that is informative,
        (lambda/(p-1) + lambda/(q-1) - 2) / lambda ,
against N on a log scale.  The fraction decays like 1/sqrt(N): finding a
revealing exponent by blind search is hopeless, which is the quantitative form
of the period-finding barrier.

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def lcm(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b


def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, isqrt(limit) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i:: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i:: i]))
    return [i for i, b in enumerate(sieve) if b]


def semiprime_data(limit: int) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    ps = primes_up_to(int(limit ** 0.5) + 200)
    ns: List[int] = []
    kstars: List[int] = []
    fracs: List[float] = []
    for i, p in enumerate(ps):
        for q in ps[i + 1:]:
            n = p * q
            if n > limit:
                break
            lam = lcm(p - 1, q - 1)
            count = lam // (p - 1) + lam // (q - 1) - 2
            ns.append(n)
            kstars.append(min(p - 1, q - 1))
            fracs.append(count / lam)
    order = np.argsort(ns)
    return (np.array(ns)[order], np.array(kstars)[order], np.array(fracs)[order])


def main() -> None:
    limit = 200_000
    ns, kstars, fracs = semiprime_data(limit)

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.2))

    ax1.scatter(ns, kstars, s=4, alpha=0.35, color="#1f3b73",

    ax2.set_title("B. Revealing exponents are vanishingly sparse\n"

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("powersum_barriers.png", dpi=160, bbox_inches="tight")
    print("wrote powersum_barriers.png")

    main()

  </div>
</div>

<div class="panel">
  <h2>3 · The master formula, live</h2>
  <p class="note" style="margin-top:0">For $k\ge 1$ the gcd depends on $k$ through two yes/no questions only:</p>
  <div class="eqbox">
    $$g_{pq}(k)\;=\;\Big(\,(p-1)\mid k\ \text{?}\ 1:p\,\Big)\;\cdot\;\Big(\,(q-1)\mid k\ \text{?}\ 1:q\,\Big)$$
  </div>
  <table id="mastertab">
    <thead><tr><th>$(p-1)\mid k$</th><th>$(q-1)\mid k$</th><th>$g_N(k)$</th><th>meaning</th>
    <th>smallest such $k$ shown</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody></tbody>
  </table>
  <details>
    <summary>Why is this true? (two moves)</summary>
    <p><b>Move 1 — residues march in formation.</b> The integers $1,\dots,pq$ cover each residue
    class modulo $p$ exactly $q$ times, so
    $$\sum_{a=1}^{pq}a^{k}\;\equiv\;q\cdot\!\!\sum_{x\bmod p}\!x^{k}\pmod p .$$
    All the complexity of the interval collapses into a single sum over $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.</p>
    <p><b>Move 2 — Fermat decides the inner sum.</b> The nonzero residues form a cyclic group of
    order $p-1$. If $(p-1)\mid k$ then $x^{k}=1$ for each of them and the sum is $p-1\equiv-1$.
    Otherwise pick a generator $g$; multiplying the sum by $g^{k}\ne 1$ permutes its terms, so
    $S=g^kS$, forcing $S=0$. Hence
    $$\sum_{x\bmod p}x^{k}=\begin{cases}-1,&(p-1)\mid k\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$</p>
    <p>Since $p\nmid q$, we get $p\mid F(k)\iff (p-1)\nmid k$; symmetrically for $q$; and
    $\gcd(\cdot,pq)=\gcd(\cdot,p)\gcd(\cdot,q)$ because $p,q$ are coprime. Done.</p>
    <p>Read at $k=p-1$: the first bracket is $1$ and the second is $q$, so one gcd computation
    returns the factor $q$. When $p<q$ the side condition $(q-1)\nmid(p-1)$ is automatic —
    a positive multiple of $q-1$ is at least $q-1>p-1$.</p>
  </details>
</div>

<div class="panel">
  <h2>4 · Reading $\lambda(N)$ — and the recovery trap</h2>
  <div id="recovery"></div>
  <details>
    <summary>The naive recovery formula, and why it fails</summary>
    <p>Since $\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)=N-(p+q)+1$, one is tempted to read $\lambda(N)$ off the
    sequence and set $p+q=N-\lambda(N)+1$, then solve $X^2-(p+q)X+N=0$. This conflates the
    <i>least common multiple</i> $\lambda(N)=\mathrm{lcm}(p-1,q-1)$ with the <i>product</i>
    $\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)$.</p>
    <p><b>Counterexample.</b> $p=5$, $q=13$, $N=65$: $\lambda=\mathrm{lcm}(4,12)=12$ and
    $65-12+1=54\neq 18=p+q$.</p>
    <p><b>The correct identity</b>, valid for all $p,q\ge1$, follows from
    $\gcd(m,n)\,\mathrm{lcm}(m,n)=mn$:
    $$\gcd(p-1,q-1)\cdot\lambda(N)\;+\;(p+q)\;=\;N+1 .$$
    Check: $\gcd(4,12)\cdot 12+18=4\cdot12+18=66=65+1$. ✓</p>
    <p>The naive form is the special case $\gcd(p-1,q-1)=1$. Note that if $p$ and $q$ are
    <i>both odd</i> then $2$ divides both $p-1$ and $q-1$, so the guard fails and the naive
    formula is wrong in every case of practical interest. It holds only when one prime is $2$
    — try $p=2$ above.</p>
  </details>
</div>

<div class="panel">
  <h2>5 · Why this is not a factoring algorithm</h2>
  <div id="cost"></div>
  <details>
    <summary>The density theorem, and the period-finding barrier</summary>
    <p>Inside one period $\lambda$, the exponents that reveal a proper factor are exactly those
    divisible by <i>exactly one</i> of $p-1$, $q-1$. The two sets of multiples inside $(0,\lambda]$
    have sizes $\lambda/(p-1)$ and $\lambda/(q-1)$ and meet only at $\lambda$ itself, so the count is
    $$\frac{\lambda}{p-1}+\frac{\lambda}{q-1}-2 .$$
    As a fraction of the period that is about $\tfrac1{p-1}+\tfrac1{q-1}\approx 2/\sqrt N$:
    negligible at cryptographic sizes.</p>
    <p>So the information is fully present and perfectly structured — the factors appear
    literally as values of an explicitly defined sequence — but each sample costs $O(N)$
    operations and the informative samples are vanishingly rare. That combination is exactly
    what a period-finding subroutine dissolves, and it is the same structure that
    <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm" target="_blank">Shor's algorithm</a>
    exploits for $x\mapsto a^{x}\bmod N$.</p>
  </details>
</div>

### A guided tour of the power-sum gcd, from one line of arithmetic to the edge of what classical computers can do

---

## 0 · The one-line definition

Everything on this page comes from a single expression. Fix a whole number $N$ and an
exponent $k$, add up the $k$-th powers of every number from $1$ to $N$, and take the
greatest common divisor of the result with $N$:

$$F_N(k) \;=\; \sum_{a=1}^{N} a^{k}, \qquad\qquad g_N(k) \;=\; \gcd\!\big(F_N(k),\, N\big).$$

That is the whole object of study. No cleverness, no choices, no randomness. And yet, as we
are about to see, this sequence is a machine that hands you the prime factorization of $N$
— twice over, in two entirely different ways.

Let us just look at it. Take $N = 35$ and compute $g_{35}(k)$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$:

$$35,\; 35,\; 35,\; \mathbf{7},\; 35,\; \mathbf{5},\; 35,\; \mathbf{7},\; 35,\; 35,\; 35,\; \mathbf{1},\; 35,\; 35, \dots$$

At position $4$ the sequence simply says **7**. At position $6$ it says **5**. And
$35 = 5 \times 7$.

> **The question this page answers.** Why? And if a factorization is sitting there in plain
> sight, why is factoring still hard?

---

## 2 · Why the sequence looks like that

There are exactly four values in the whole spectrum, and which one you get depends on two
yes/no questions. Here is the statement, and then the two-move proof.

> **Theorem (master value table).** Let $N = pq$ with $p \ne q$ prime, and let $k \ge 1$.
> Then
> $$g_N(k) \;=\; \Big(\text{$1$ if $(p-1)\mid k$, else $p$}\Big)\cdot\Big(\text{$1$ if $(q-1)\mid k$, else $q$}\Big).$$

| $(p-1)\mid k$ | $(q-1)\mid k$ | $g_N(k)$ | what you see |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| no | no | $N$ | grey — no information |
| yes | no | $q$ | **a factor** |
| no | yes | $p$ | **a factor** |
| yes | yes | $1$ | white — no information |

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof — it is two moves, and both fit in your head</summary>

**Move 1 — the residues march in formation.**
The numbers $1, 2, \dots, N$ with $N = pq$ hit every residue class modulo $p$ exactly $q$
times. (Walk along the interval: $1, 2, \dots, p$ covers all $p$ classes once; the next
block of $p$ covers them again; there are $q$ blocks.) So when we reduce the power sum
modulo $p$, the whole interval collapses to a single residue-system sum:
$$F_N(k) \;\equiv\; q \cdot \!\!\sum_{x \bmod p}\! x^{k} \pmod p .$$

**Move 2 — Fermat evaluates the inner sum.**
The nonzero residues modulo $p$ form a cyclic group of order $p-1$.

- If $(p-1) \mid k$, then $x^{k} = 1$ for every one of them by
  [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_little_theorem),
  so the sum is $p - 1 \equiv -1$.
- If not, pick a generator $g$. Then $g^{k} \ne 1$, and $x \mapsto gx$ merely permutes the
  units, so the sum $S$ satisfies $g^{k}S = S$. Hence $(g^{k}-1)S = 0$, and since
  $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is a field, $S = 0$.

So $\sum_{x \bmod p} x^{k}$ is $-1$ or $0$, on the nose.

**Putting them together.** $p \nmid q$, so $q \cdot (-1) \not\equiv 0$ and
$q \cdot 0 \equiv 0$. Therefore
$$p \mid F_N(k) \iff (p-1) \nmid k,$$
and symmetrically for $q$. Finally $\gcd(\cdot, pq) = \gcd(\cdot, p)\gcd(\cdot, q)$ because
$p$ and $q$ are coprime. That is the table. $\blacksquare$

</details>

**The headline corollary.** Set $k = p-1$. The first bracket becomes $1$; the second stays
$q$ as long as $(q-1) \nmid (p-1)$. And if $p < q$ that condition is *free* — a positive
multiple of $q-1$ is at least $q-1 > p-1$. So:

> **Theorem (unconditional factor reveal).** For distinct primes $p < q$,
> $$\gcd\Big(\textstyle\sum_{a=1}^{pq} a^{\,p-1},\; pq\Big) \;=\; q .$$

One sum. One gcd. One factor.

## 4 · Interlude: the method that has no bad base

The classical relative of this idea is
[Pollard's $p-1$ method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollard%27s_p_%E2%88%92_1_algorithm):
choose a base $a$, compute $\gcd(a^{M}-1, N)$, and hope. The hope is real. A bad base
tells you nothing and you must start over.

The power sum has no base to choose. It aggregates *every* residue at once, and Fermat's
theorem knows the exact value of that aggregate. So the failure mode simply does not exist.
To make the contrast sharp, here is a base that fails not sometimes but always.

> **Theorem (a universally bad Pollard base).** Let $N = pq$ with $p \ne q$ distinct odd
> primes. Then for *every* exponent $M$,
> $$\gcd\big((N-1)^{M}-1,\; N\big) \;=\; \begin{cases} N, & M \text{ even},\\ 1, & M \text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$
> It is never a proper factor. Not once.

<details>
<summary>Why this base is doomed — and why it is nonetheless a legitimate choice</summary>

The base $a = N-1$ satisfies $1 < a < N$ and $\gcd(a, N) = 1$: a practitioner would happily
select it. But $N - 1 \equiv -1$ modulo *every* prime factor of $N$ simultaneously. So
$(N-1)^{M} - 1 \equiv (-1)^{M} - 1$ modulo each of $p$ and $q$ — which is $0$ modulo both
when $M$ is even, and $-2$ (hence nonzero, since $p, q$ are odd) modulo both when $M$ is
odd. The two local conditions are locked together and can never be separated, which is
exactly what Pollard needs.

The moral: base-dependence is not a minor inconvenience. It admits *permanent* failure for
perfectly reasonable choices. Base-freeness is a structural property, not a convenience.

</details>

## 5 · The second encoding: the period, and a formula that is false

So much for the values. Now the rhythm.

Because the master formula depends on $k$ only through two divisibility predicates, the
spectrum is periodic. Its period is the
[Carmichael function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_function)
$$\lambda(N) \;=\; \operatorname{lcm}(p-1,\, q-1).$$

> **Theorem (periodicity, sharply).** For $k \ge 1$,
> $g_N(k + \lambda(N)) = g_N(k)$; moreover $g_N(k) = 1$ **exactly** when
> $\lambda(N) \mid k$; consequently $\lambda(N)$ is the least $k \ge 1$ with $g_N(k) = 1$,
> and no positive integer smaller than $\lambda(N)$ is a period.

So $\lambda(N)$ is *legible*: read down the spectrum to the first white cell, and its
position is the Carmichael number of $N$.

Now the trap. Since $\varphi(N) = (p-1)(q-1) = N - (p+q) + 1$, it is very tempting to write
$p + q = N - \lambda(N) + 1$, then recover $p$ and $q$ from their sum and product. This is
wrong, and the way it is wrong is instructive.

> **The counterexample.** $p = 5$, $q = 13$, $N = 65$. Then
> $\lambda(65) = \operatorname{lcm}(4, 12) = 12$, and $65 - 12 + 1 = 54$. But $p + q = 18$.

The error is conflating the *least common multiple* $\lambda(N)$ with the *product*
$\varphi(N)$. They differ by exactly the gcd.

> **Theorem (corrected recovery identity).** For all integers $p, q \ge 1$, with
> $\lambda = \operatorname{lcm}(p-1, q-1)$,
> $$\gcd(p-1,\,q-1)\cdot\lambda \;+\; (p+q) \;=\; pq + 1 .$$
> Check: $\gcd(4,12)\cdot 12 + 18 = 4\cdot 12 + 18 = 66 = 65 + 1$. ✓

<details>
<summary>The proof, and the sting in the tail</summary>

**Proof.** The identity $\gcd(m,n)\operatorname{lcm}(m,n) = mn$ with $m = p-1$, $n = q-1$
turns the first term into $(p-1)(q-1)$. Writing $p = a+1$ and $q = b+1$, the claim becomes
$ab + (a+1) + (b+1) = (a+1)(b+1) + 1$, a polynomial identity. $\blacksquare$

**The sting.** The naive formula is the special case $\gcd(p-1,q-1) = 1$. But if $p$ and
$q$ are *both odd*, then $2$ divides both $p-1$ and $q-1$, so that gcd is at least $2$ and
the guard **always fails**. It holds only when one of the primes is $2$. In other words,
the naive formula is not occasionally wrong — it is wrong in every case anyone cares about.
Go back to the widget and try to find a pair of odd primes where the guard is satisfied.
You will not.

**What survives.** Under the guard, recovery genuinely works: if $a \le b$ satisfy $ab = N$
and $a + b = N + 1 - \lambda$, then $(a,b) = (p,q)$, because a pair of numbers is determined
by its sum and product (Vieta). Try $p = 2$ in the widget to see this succeed.

</details>

## 6 · So why is factoring still hard?

We now have a sequence that displays the factors of $N$ as literal values, and whose period
determines the factorization outright. Why is $N$ safe?

Two obstacles, and both are theorems.

**Obstacle one: sampling is expensive.** Computing $F_N(k)$ from the definition costs
$O(N)$ modular operations. The first exponent that does anything is
$k^\ast = \min(p-1, q-1)$ — this is exactly the least such exponent, and it satisfies
$(k^\ast+1)^2 \le N$, so $k^\ast < \sqrt N$. Total: $O(N^{3/2})$. Trial division is
$O(\sqrt N)$. **The method is worse than the most naive method there is.**

**Obstacle two: informative exponents are vanishingly rare.**

> **Theorem (density).** Inside one period $\lambda$, the number of exponents that reveal a
> proper factor is exactly
> $$\frac{\lambda}{p-1} + \frac{\lambda}{q-1} - 2 .$$

<details>
<summary>Where that count comes from</summary>

An exponent is revealing precisely when it is divisible by *exactly one* of $p-1$, $q-1$
(if by neither you get $N$, if by both you get $1$). Inside $(0, \lambda]$ there are
$\lambda/(p-1)$ multiples of $p-1$ and $\lambda/(q-1)$ multiples of $q-1$, and the two sets
meet only at $\lambda$ itself — because a common multiple is a multiple of the lcm, which
is $\lambda$. The symmetric difference therefore has
$|A| + |B| - 2|A\cap B| = \lambda/(p-1) + \lambda/(q-1) - 2$ elements. $\blacksquare$

</details>

As a fraction of the period that is about $\frac{1}{p-1} + \frac{1}{q-1} \approx 2/\sqrt N$.
Both barriers, over every semiprime below $200{,}000$:

{{visualization:1}}

This is the whole story in one sentence: **the factorization is not concealed, it is
displayed — but reading it requires either $O(N)$ work per sample or knowing where to look,
and knowing where to look means knowing $p-1$ or $q-1$, which means knowing the answer.**

That is precisely the wall a quantum computer walks through.
[Shor's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm) is a period-finding
machine: it extracts the period of a modular-exponential sequence in polynomial time.
Here we have a *different* sequence with the same signature — an explicit function of $k$
whose least period is the Carmichael number and whose period therefore yields the
factorization. Same structure; the entire difficulty concentrated in one operation.

## 7 · Two surprises at the edges

The theory does not stop at semiprimes, and the extensions each contain a genuine surprise.

### 7a · Carmichael numbers are the exact blind spot

Nothing in §2 used the number of prime factors. For any squarefree $N$ and prime $p \mid N$,
$p \mid F_N(k) \iff (p-1) \nmid k$, so $\gcd(F_N(k), N) = 1$ exactly when
$\lambda(N) = \operatorname{lcm}_{p \mid N}(p-1)$ divides $k$.

Now apply that at the most natural exponent of all, $k = N-1$. The condition
$\lambda(N) \mid N-1$ unfolds into "$(p-1) \mid (N-1)$ for every prime $p \mid N$" — which
is *precisely*
[Korselt's criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number) defining
[Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number).

> **Theorem (Korselt bridge).** A squarefree $N \ge 2$ satisfies Korselt's criterion if and
> only if $\gcd\big(F_N(N-1),\, N\big) = 1$.

In words: **Carmichael numbers are exactly the squarefree moduli on which this method, at
the one exponent you would naturally try, tells you nothing at all.** The same divisibility
that lets them fool the Fermat primality test lets them defeat the reveal. The smallest is
$561 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17$, with $\lambda = \operatorname{lcm}(2,10,16) = 80 \mid 560$.

The following script checks the equivalence on every squarefree composite below $3000$ —
and shows that the blindness is specific to the exponent $N-1$, not global:

{{demo:2}}

### 7b · The prime powers do something unexpected

If $N$ is not squarefree, you would guess that the relevant condition at a prime power
$p^{e}$ involves $\lambda(p^{e}) = p^{e-1}(p-1)$, the exponent of the unit group. It does
not.

> **Theorem (prime-power evaluation).** For an odd prime $p$, $e \ge 1$, $k \ge 1$,
> $$\sum_{a < p^{e}} a^{k} \;\equiv\; \begin{cases} -p^{\,e-1} \pmod{p^{e}} & \text{if } (p-1)\mid k,\\ 0 \pmod{p^{e}} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
> Hence for $N = p^{e}m$ with $p \nmid m$, the gcd of $F_N(k)$ with $p^{e}$ is $p^{e-1}$
> when $(p-1) \mid k$ and $p^{e}$ otherwise.

The governing condition is $(p-1) \mid k$, **not** $\lambda(p^{e}) \mid k$. Concretely: for
$p^{e} = 9$ the sum is $\equiv -3$ for *every even* $k$, not merely for $k$ divisible by
$\lambda(9) = 6$. The $p$-part of the unit group is invisible to the power sum.

<details>
<summary>The mechanism: lifting the exponent, and why the prime 2 escapes</summary>

Write each $a < p^{e}$ uniquely as $a = p^{e-1}j + r$ with $j < p$ and $r < p^{e-1}$.
Modulo $p^{e}$ we have $(p^{e-1})^2 = 0$, so the binomial expansion truncates after two
terms:
$$(r + p^{e-1}j)^{k} \;=\; r^{k} + k\,r^{k-1}\,p^{e-1}j .$$
Summing over $r$ and then over $j$: the first part gives $p\sum_{r} r^{k}$, and the second
carries the factor
$$p^{e-1}\sum_{j<p} j \;=\; p^{e-1}\cdot\frac{p(p-1)}{2}.$$
Now $p(p-1)/2$ is a multiple of $p$ **exactly because $p$ is odd** (the $2$ in the
denominator is absorbed by $p-1$). So the second part is a multiple of $p^{e}$ and
vanishes, leaving the clean recursion
$$\sum_{a<p^{e}} a^{k} \;\equiv\; p \sum_{a<p^{e-1}} a^{k} \pmod{p^{e}},$$
which unwinds by induction with the Fermat evaluation as the base case. The condition
$(p-1)\mid k$ is set at the base and never touched again — that is why the $p$-part is
invisible.

And that is exactly why $2$ is exceptional: for $p = 2$ we have $p(p-1)/2 = 1$, not a
multiple of $2$, and the argument collapses. Indeed for $N = 8$ and $k \ge 2$ the gcd is
$4$ for even $k$ and $8$ for odd $k$ — no analogue of the odd formula. Pinning down the
$2$-part in general is open.

</details>

## 9 · What to take away

We started with an algorithm and ended with a structure theorem.

$\gcd\big(\sum_{a=1}^{N} a^{k},\, N\big)$ is not a heuristic that sometimes works. It is a
function of $k$ whose value is known in closed form, whose zeros and ones are dictated by
Fermat's little theorem, whose least period is the Carmichael function, and whose blind
spots are precisely the Carmichael numbers. Along the way it corrects a false folklore
recovery formula and identifies the exact missing datum, $\gcd(p-1, q-1)$.

As a factoring algorithm it loses to trial division. As a lens, it is superb: it shows that
the secret is not hidden. It is written down, in order, in an integer sequence anyone can
define in one line. It is just written in a rhythm too slow to hear.

That gap — between *encoded* and *accessible* — is the whole subject.

/-!
# Robustness: the power sum has no "bad base", Pollard's `p-1` does

Pollard's `p-1` method depends on a *base* `a`: it computes `gcd (a^M - 1, N)` and
succeeds only if the multiplicative order of `a` modulo one prime factor divides the
exponent `M` while the order modulo the other one does not.  The power-sum quantity
`powerSum N k = ∑_{a=1}^{N} a^k` has no base parameter at all: it aggregates every
residue simultaneously.

This file makes the contrast precise.

* `PowerSumReveal.pollard_universally_bad_base` — for a semiprime `N = p*q` of distinct
  *odd* primes, the base `a = N - 1` (a nontrivial base, coprime to `N`) is bad for
  **every** exponent `M ≥ 1`: `gcd (a^M - 1, N) ∈ {1, N}`, never a proper factor.
* `PowerSumReveal.powerSum_succeeds_where_pollard_fails` — at the very exponent
  `k = p - 1` where that base makes Pollard return the useless value `N`, the power
  sum returns the factor `q` (under the standard side condition `(q-1) ∤ (p-1)`).
* `PowerSumReveal.pollard_bad_base_example` — the concrete instance `N = 35`, `M = 4`,
  `a = 6`: Pollard returns `35`, the power sum returns `7`.

Note that the statement `a = N - 1` is a genuinely nontrivial base: `1 < N - 1 < N`.
-/

namespace PowerSumReveal

open Finset

variable {p q : ℕ}

/-- Pollard `p-1` style gcd for base `a` and exponent `M`. -/
def pollardGcd (N a M : ℕ) : ℕ := Nat.gcd (a ^ M - 1) N

/-- Casting `(N-1)^M - 1` into `ZMod p`. -/
lemma cast_pow_pred_sub_one (r N M : ℕ) [NeZero r] (hN : 2 ≤ N) :
    (((N - 1) ^ M - 1 : ℕ) : ZMod r) = ((N : ZMod r) - 1) ^ M - 1 := by
  have h1 : 1 ≤ (N - 1) ^ M := Nat.one_le_pow _ _ (by omega)
  rw [Nat.cast_sub h1]
  push_cast [Nat.cast_sub (show 1 ≤ N by omega)]
  ring

/-- For an odd prime factor `r` of `N` and an *odd* exponent `M`, the prime `r` does not
divide `(N-1)^M - 1`, because that quantity is `≡ -2 (mod r)`. -/
lemma not_dvd_pow_pred_sub_one_of_odd {r N M : ℕ} (hr : r.Prime) (hr2 : r ≠ 2)
    (hrN : r ∣ N) (hN : 2 ≤ N) (hM : Odd M) :
    ¬ r ∣ ((N - 1) ^ M - 1) := by
  haveI : Fact r.Prime := ⟨hr⟩
  intro hdvd
  have h0 : (((N - 1) ^ M - 1 : ℕ) : ZMod r) = 0 := (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff _ r).2 hdvd
  rw [cast_pow_pred_sub_one r N M hN, (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff N r).2 hrN, zero_sub,
    hM.neg_one_pow] at h0
  have h2 : ((2 : ℕ) : ZMod r) = 0 := by
    have : (-1 : ZMod r) - 1 = -(2 : ZMod r) := by ring
    rw [this] at h0
    have := neg_eq_zero.mp h0
    exact_mod_cast this
  exact hr2 ((Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hr Nat.prime_two).1
    ((ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff 2 r).1 h2))

/-- For an even exponent `M`, every divisor of `N` divides `(N-1)^M - 1`. -/
lemma dvd_pow_pred_sub_one_of_even {r N M : ℕ} (hr : r.Prime) (hrN : r ∣ N) (hN : 2 ≤ N)
    (hM : Even M) : r ∣ ((N - 1) ^ M - 1) := by
  haveI : Fact r.Prime := ⟨hr⟩
  refine (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff _ r).1 ?_
  rw [cast_pow_pred_sub_one r N M hN, (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff N r).2 hrN, zero_sub,
    hM.neg_one_pow, sub_self]

/-- **Theorem 2a (a universally bad Pollard base).**  Let `N = p * q` with `p ≠ q`
distinct odd primes.  Then the nontrivial base `a = N - 1` never reveals a factor:
for every exponent `M`, `pollardGcd N (N-1) M` is `N` (when `M` is even) or `1`
(when `M` is odd).  In particular it is never a proper divisor of `N`. -/
theorem pollard_universally_bad_base (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q)
    (hp2 : p ≠ 2) (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (M : ℕ) :
    pollardGcd (p * q) (p * q - 1) M = if Even M then p * q else 1 := by
  have hN : 2 ≤ p * q := by
    have := hp.two_le; have := hq.two_le; nlinarith
  have hcop : Nat.Coprime p q := (Nat.coprime_primes hp hq).2 hpq
  have hpN : p ∣ p * q := ⟨q, rfl⟩
  have hqN : q ∣ p * q := ⟨p, by ring⟩
  unfold pollardGcd
  rw [Nat.Coprime.gcd_mul _ hcop, gcd_prime_eq hp, gcd_prime_eq hq]
  rcases Nat.even_or_odd M with hM | hM
  · rw [if_pos hM, if_pos (dvd_pow_pred_sub_one_of_even hp hpN hN hM),
      if_pos (dvd_pow_pred_sub_one_of_even hq hqN hN hM)]
  · rw [if_neg (Nat.not_even_iff_odd.2 hM),
      if_neg (not_dvd_pow_pred_sub_one_of_odd hp hp2 hpN hN hM),
      if_neg (not_dvd_pow_pred_sub_one_of_odd hq hq2 hqN hN hM), one_mul]

/-- The bad base is genuinely nontrivial: `1 < N - 1 < N` and it is coprime to `N`. -/
theorem pollard_bad_base_nontrivial (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hp2 : p ≠ 2)
    (hq2 : q ≠ 2) :
    1 < p * q - 1 ∧ p * q - 1 < p * q ∧ Nat.Coprime (p * q - 1) (p * q) := by
  have h1 := hp.two_le
  have h2 := hq.two_le
  have h3 : 3 ≤ p := by omega
  have h4 : 3 ≤ q := by omega
  have hN : 9 ≤ p * q := by nlinarith
  refine ⟨by omega, by omega, ?_⟩
  obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ : ∃ m, p * q = m + 1 := ⟨p * q - 1, by omega⟩
  rw [hm]; simp

/-- **Theorem 2b (robustness).**  At the exponent `k = p - 1`, Pollard's method with the
bad base `N - 1` returns the useless value `N`, while the base-free power sum returns the
proper factor `q`. -/
theorem powerSum_succeeds_where_pollard_fails (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q)
    (hp2 : p ≠ 2) (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hdvd : ¬ (q - 1) ∣ (p - 1)) :
    pollardGcd (p * q) (p * q - 1) (p - 1) = p * q ∧
      Nat.gcd (powerSum (p * q) (p - 1)) (p * q) = q := by
  have hodd : Odd p := hp.odd_of_ne_two hp2
  have heven : Even (p - 1) := by
    obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := hodd
    refine ⟨m, by omega⟩
  refine ⟨?_, powerSum_factor_reveal hp hq hpq hdvd⟩
  rw [pollard_universally_bad_base hp hq hpq hp2 hq2, if_pos heven]

/-- **Concrete instance.**  `N = 35 = 5 * 7`, exponent `M = 4 = p - 1`.
Pollard's `p-1` with the base `6 = N - 1` returns `35` (failure); the power sum at the
same exponent returns the factor `7`. -/
theorem pollard_bad_base_example :
    pollardGcd 35 6 4 = 35 ∧ Nat.gcd (powerSum 35 4) 35 = 7 := by
  constructor
  · decide
  · have h : (35 : ℕ) = 5 * 7 := by norm_num
    have := powerSum_factor_reveal (p := 5) (q := 7) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
      (by norm_num) (by decide)
    simpa [h] using this

/-!
# Power-sum GCD factor reveal

For a modulus `N` put

`powerSum N k = ∑_{a = 1}^{N} a ^ k`.

The main result of this file is a *complete* description of `gcd (powerSum N k) N`
when `N = p * q` is a semiprime and `k ≥ 1`:

`gcd (powerSum (p*q) k, p*q) = (if (p-1) ∣ k then 1 else p) * (if (q-1) ∣ k then 1 else q)`.

The mechanism is a two-step reduction.

* *Periodicity.* The interval `[1, N]` with `N = p * m` covers every residue class
  modulo `p` exactly `m` times, so `powerSum (p*m) k ≡ m * ∑_{x ∈ ZMod p} x^k (mod p)`.
* *Fermat.* For `k ≥ 1`, `∑_{x ∈ ZMod p} x^k = -1` if `(p-1) ∣ k` and `= 0` otherwise.

Consequently `p ∣ powerSum (p*m) k ↔ ¬ (p-1) ∣ k` (when `p ∤ m`), and the gcd formula
follows from multiplicativity of `Nat.gcd` over coprime factors.

Specialising to `k = p - 1` gives the advertised **factor reveal**:
`gcd (powerSum (p*q) (p-1), p*q) = q` whenever `(q-1) ∤ (p-1)`.

## Main results

* `PowerSumReveal.sum_pow_zmod` — Fermat power-sum over `ZMod p`.
* `PowerSumReveal.powerSum_cast` — the periodicity reduction, in `ZMod p`.
* `PowerSumReveal.prime_dvd_powerSum_iff` — divisibility criterion.
* `PowerSumReveal.gcd_powerSum_semiprime` — the master gcd formula.
* `PowerSumReveal.powerSum_factor_reveal` — Theorem 1 (factor reveal at `k = p-1`).
-/

namespace PowerSumReveal

open Finset

/-- `powerSum N k = ∑_{a=1}^{N} a ^ k`, the `k`-th power sum of a complete residue
system modulo `N`. -/
def powerSum (N k : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ a ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, a ^ k

@[simp] lemma powerSum_zero_exp (N : ℕ) : powerSum N 0 = N := by
  simp [powerSum]

/-! ## Step 1: the Fermat power sum over `ZMod p` -/

/-- **Fermat power sum.**  For a prime `p` and `k ≥ 1`,
`∑_{x : ZMod p} x ^ k = -1` when `(p-1) ∣ k` and `0` otherwise. -/
theorem sum_pow_zmod (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    ∑ x : ZMod p, x ^ k = if (p - 1) ∣ k then -1 else 0 := by
  classical
  have hcard : Fintype.card (ZMod p) = p := ZMod.card p
  let φ : (ZMod p)ˣ ↪ ZMod p := ⟨fun x ↦ x, Units.val_injective⟩
  have hmap : univ.map φ = univ \ {0} := by
    ext x
    simpa only [mem_map, mem_univ, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk, true_and, mem_sdiff,
      mem_singleton, φ] using isUnit_iff_ne_zero
  calc ∑ x : ZMod p, x ^ k = ∑ x ∈ univ \ {(0 : ZMod p)}, x ^ k := by
        rw [← sum_sdiff ({0} : Finset (ZMod p)).subset_univ, sum_singleton, zero_pow hk,
          add_zero]
    _ = ∑ x : (ZMod p)ˣ, ((x : ZMod p) ^ k) := by simp [φ, ← hmap, univ.sum_map φ]
    _ = if (p - 1) ∣ k then -1 else 0 := by
        rw [FiniteField.sum_pow_units (ZMod p) k, hcard]

/-! ## Step 2: periodicity of `a ↦ a mod p` on an interval of length `p * m` -/

/-- Summing a function of `a mod p` over one full period `range p` is the same as
summing over `ZMod p`. -/
theorem sum_range_modCast (p : ℕ) [NeZero p] (f : ZMod p → ZMod p) :
    ∑ a ∈ range p, f (a : ZMod p) = ∑ x : ZMod p, f x := by
  refine Finset.sum_nbij' (i := fun a => ((a : ZMod p))) (j := fun x => x.val) ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_
  · intro a _; simp
  · intro x _; simp [ZMod.val_lt]
  · intro a ha; simp only [mem_range] at ha; simp [ZMod.val_natCast_of_lt ha]
  · intro x _; simp
  · intro _ _; rfl

/-- Over `m` full periods the residues repeat, so the sum is `m` copies of the
sum over `ZMod p`. -/
theorem sum_range_mul_modCast (p : ℕ) [NeZero p] (f : ZMod p → ZMod p) (m : ℕ) :
    ∑ a ∈ range (p * m), f (a : ZMod p) = m • ∑ x : ZMod p, f x := by
  induction m with
  | zero => simp
  | succ m ih =>
      have hpm : p * (m + 1) = p * m + p := by ring
      have base : ∑ a ∈ range p, f ((p * m + a : ℕ) : ZMod p) = ∑ x : ZMod p, f x := by
        have hshift : ∀ a : ℕ, ((p * m + a : ℕ) : ZMod p) = (a : ZMod p) := by
          intro a; push_cast [ZMod.natCast_self]; ring
        simp only [hshift]
        exact sum_range_modCast p f
      rw [hpm, Finset.sum_range_add, ih, base, succ_nsmul]

/-- The interval `[1, N]` and the interval `[0, N)` have the same `k`-th power sum
modulo `p` whenever `k ≥ 1` and `p ∣ N`. -/
theorem powerSum_cast_eq_range (p N : ℕ) [NeZero p] {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≠ 0)
    (hN : (N : ZMod p) = 0) :
    ((powerSum N k : ℕ) : ZMod p) = ∑ a ∈ range N, (a : ZMod p) ^ k := by
  have hcast : ((powerSum N k : ℕ) : ZMod p) = ∑ a ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, (a : ZMod p) ^ k := by
    unfold powerSum; push_cast; rfl
  rw [hcast]
  have hins : range (N + 1) = insert 0 (Finset.Icc 1 N) := by
    ext x; simp only [mem_range, Finset.mem_insert, Finset.mem_Icc]; omega
  have hnot : (0 : ℕ) ∉ Finset.Icc 1 N := by simp
  have h1 : ∑ a ∈ range (N + 1), (a : ZMod p) ^ k
      = (0 : ZMod p) ^ k + ∑ a ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, (a : ZMod p) ^ k := by
    rw [hins, Finset.sum_insert hnot]; norm_num
  have h2 : ∑ a ∈ range (N + 1), (a : ZMod p) ^ k
      = ∑ a ∈ range N, (a : ZMod p) ^ k + (N : ZMod p) ^ k := Finset.sum_range_succ _ N
  rw [zero_pow hk, zero_add] at h1
  rw [hN, zero_pow hk, add_zero] at h2
  rw [← h1, h2]

/-- **Periodicity reduction.**  For `N = p * m` and `k ≥ 1`,
`powerSum N k ≡ m * ∑_{x : ZMod p} x^k (mod p)`. -/
theorem powerSum_cast (p m : ℕ) [NeZero p] {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    ((powerSum (p * m) k : ℕ) : ZMod p) = (m : ZMod p) * ∑ x : ZMod p, x ^ k := by
  have hN : ((p * m : ℕ) : ZMod p) = 0 := by push_cast [ZMod.natCast_self]; ring
  rw [powerSum_cast_eq_range p (p * m) hk hN,
    sum_range_mul_modCast p (fun x => x ^ k) m, nsmul_eq_mul]

/-! ## Step 3: the divisibility criterion -/

/-- **Divisibility criterion.**  If `p` is prime, `p ∤ m` and `k ≥ 1`, then
`p ∣ powerSum (p * m) k` exactly when `(p-1) ∤ k`. -/
theorem prime_dvd_powerSum_iff {p m k : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpm : ¬ p ∣ m) (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    p ∣ powerSum (p * m) k ↔ ¬ (p - 1) ∣ k := by
  haveI : Fact p.Prime := ⟨hp⟩
  have hcast := powerSum_cast p m hk
  rw [sum_pow_zmod p hk] at hcast
  have hmne : (m : ZMod p) ≠ 0 := fun h => hpm ((ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff m p).1 h)
  constructor
  · intro hdvd hdk
    have h0 : ((powerSum (p * m) k : ℕ) : ZMod p) = 0 :=
      (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff _ p).2 hdvd
    rw [hcast, if_pos hdk] at h0
    exact hmne (by simpa using h0)
  · intro hdk
    refine (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff _ p).1 ?_
    rw [hcast, if_neg hdk, mul_zero]

/-! ## Step 4: the gcd formula -/

/-- `gcd n p` for a prime `p` is `p` or `1` according to divisibility. -/
theorem gcd_prime_eq {n p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) : Nat.gcd n p = if p ∣ n then p else 1 := by
  split <;> rename_i h
  · exact Nat.gcd_eq_right h
  · exact Nat.Coprime.gcd_eq_one ((Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd hp).2 h).symm

/-- **Master formula.**  For a semiprime `N = p * q` with `p ≠ q` and `k ≥ 1`, the gcd
`gcd (powerSum N k) N` is determined by which of `p-1`, `q-1` divide `k`. -/
theorem gcd_powerSum_semiprime {p q k : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q)
    (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    Nat.gcd (powerSum (p * q) k) (p * q)
      = (if (p - 1) ∣ k then 1 else p) * (if (q - 1) ∣ k then 1 else q) := by

/-- Splitting a range of length `M * t` into `t` blocks of length `M`. -/
theorem sum_range_block {R : Type*} [AddCommMonoid R] (M : ℕ) (f : ℕ → R) (t : ℕ) :

  induction t with

  | succ t ih =>

      rw [h, Finset.sum_range_add, ih, Finset.sum_range_succ]

  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
      have h : (x + y) ^ (k + 2) = (x + y) ^ (k + 1) * (x + y) := by ring
      rw [h, ih]; push_cast; linear_combination ((k : R) + 1) * x ^ k * hy

# The power-sum reveal for arbitrary squarefree moduli, and a Giuga/Korselt bridge

The semiprime analysis of `Geometry.PowerSumFactorReveal` uses nothing about the
number of prime factors: for **any** squarefree `N` and any prime `p ∣ N`,

`p ∣ powerSum N k ↔ ¬ (p - 1) ∣ k`   (`k ≥ 1`).

`λ(N) = lcm_{p ∣ N} (p - 1)` is the Carmichael function of a squarefree number.
This is the general form of the "Carmichael periodicity" phenomenon.

* *Fermat/Giuga.*  For a prime `p`, `powerSum p (p-1) ≡ -1 (mod p)`.
* *Korselt.*  A squarefree `N` is a Korselt number (`(p-1) ∣ (N-1)` for all `p ∣ N`,

  exponent `k = N - 1` is trivial.  So Carmichael numbers are precisely the squarefree
  moduli on which the exponent `N-1` gives the method no information.

* `PowerSumReveal.prime_dvd_powerSum_iff_squarefree`
* `PowerSumReveal.coprime_powerSum_iff_lambda_dvd`

* `PowerSumReveal.korselt_iff_coprime_powerSum`

namespace PowerSumReveal

open Finset

/-- The Carmichael function of a squarefree modulus: `lcm_{p ∣ N} (p - 1)`. -/
def lambdaSqfree (N : ℕ) : ℕ := N.primeFactors.lcm (fun p => p - 1)

/-- In a squarefree number, a prime factor appears to the first power only. -/
lemma not_dvd_div_of_squarefree {N p : ℕ} (hN : Squarefree N) (hp : p.Prime) (hd : p ∣ N) :
    ¬ p ∣ N / p := by
  intro h2
  have hsq : p * p ∣ N := by
    obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := hd
    obtain ⟨d, hdd⟩ := h2
    subst hc
    rw [Nat.mul_div_cancel_left _ hp.pos] at hdd
    exact ⟨d, by rw [hdd]; ring⟩
  exact hp.one_lt.ne' (Nat.isUnit_iff.mp (hN p hsq))

/-- **Divisibility criterion, squarefree case.**  For squarefree `N`, a prime `p ∣ N`
and `k ≥ 1`: `p ∣ powerSum N k ↔ ¬ (p-1) ∣ k`. -/
theorem prime_dvd_powerSum_iff_squarefree {N p k : ℕ} (hN : Squarefree N) (hp : p.Prime)
    (hd : p ∣ N) (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    p ∣ powerSum N k ↔ ¬ (p - 1) ∣ k := by
  obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := hd
  have hpm : ¬ p ∣ m := by
    have := not_dvd_div_of_squarefree hN hp ⟨m, hm⟩
    rwa [hm, Nat.mul_div_cancel_left _ hp.pos] at this
  rw [hm]
  exact prime_dvd_powerSum_iff hp hpm hk

/-- **General Carmichael periodicity.**  For squarefree `N > 0` and `k ≥ 1`, the power sum
is coprime to `N` exactly when `λ(N) ∣ k`. -/
theorem coprime_powerSum_iff_lambda_dvd {N k : ℕ} (hN : Squarefree N) (hN0 : N ≠ 0)
    (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    Nat.Coprime (powerSum N k) N ↔ lambdaSqfree N ∣ k := by
  rw [lambdaSqfree, Finset.lcm_dvd_iff]
  constructor
  · intro hcop r hr
    rw [Nat.mem_primeFactors] at hr
    obtain ⟨hrp, hrN, -⟩ := hr
    by_contra hdk
    have hdvd : r ∣ powerSum N k :=
      (prime_dvd_powerSum_iff_squarefree hN hrp hrN hk).2 hdk
    exact Nat.Prime.not_coprime_iff_dvd.2 ⟨r, hrp, hdvd, hrN⟩ hcop
  · intro hall
    by_contra hcop
    obtain ⟨r, hrp, hrS, hrN⟩ := Nat.Prime.not_coprime_iff_dvd.1 hcop
    have hmem : r ∈ N.primeFactors := Nat.mem_primeFactors.2 ⟨hrp, hrN, hN0⟩
    exact (prime_dvd_powerSum_iff_squarefree hN hrp hrN hk).1 hrS (hall r hmem)

/-- **Fermat / Giuga direction.**  For a prime `p`, `∑_{a=1}^{p} a^{p-1} ≡ -1 (mod p)`. -/
theorem powerSum_prime_eq_neg_one {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    ((powerSum p (p - 1) : ℕ) : ZMod p) = -1 := by
  haveI : Fact p.Prime := ⟨hp⟩
  have hk : p - 1 ≠ 0 := by have := hp.two_le; omega
  have h := powerSum_cast p 1 (k := p - 1) hk
  rw [mul_one] at h
  rw [sum_pow_zmod p hk, if_pos dvd_rfl] at h
  simpa using h

/-- Consequently a prime is never "revealed" by itself: the gcd is `1`. -/
theorem gcd_powerSum_prime {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    Nat.gcd (powerSum p (p - 1)) p = 1 := by
  haveI : Fact p.Prime := ⟨hp⟩
  have hne : ((powerSum p (p - 1) : ℕ) : ZMod p) ≠ 0 := by
    rw [powerSum_prime_eq_neg_one hp]
    simp
  have : ¬ p ∣ powerSum p (p - 1) := fun h => hne ((ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff _ p).2 h)
  rw [gcd_prime_eq hp, if_neg this]

/-- **Korselt bridge.**  A squarefree `N ≥ 2` satisfies Korselt's criterion — the
condition defining Carmichael numbers, `(p-1) ∣ (N-1)` for every prime `p ∣ N` — if and
only if the power-sum gcd at exponent `N - 1` is trivial.  Equivalently, Carmichael
numbers are exactly the squarefree moduli that defeat the reveal at `k = N-1`. -/
theorem korselt_iff_coprime_powerSum {N : ℕ} (hN : Squarefree N) (hN2 : 2 ≤ N) :
    (∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, (p - 1) ∣ (N - 1)) ↔
      Nat.gcd (powerSum N (N - 1)) N = 1 := by
  have hk : N - 1 ≠ 0 := by omega
  have h := coprime_powerSum_iff_lambda_dvd hN (by omega) hk
  rw [Nat.Coprime] at h
  rw [h, lambdaSqfree, Finset.lcm_dvd_iff]

*Original guess (falsified).* $\gcd(F(k), N) = \prod p^{\,e_p - [\lambda(p^{e_p})\,\mid\, k]}$

$\lambda(9) = 6$.

*Corrected statement, now a theorem.* For an odd prime $p$, $e \ge 1$, $k \ge 1$,
$$\sum_{a < p^e} a^k \equiv -p^{\,e-1} \pmod{p^e} \ \text{ if } (p-1) \mid k, \qquad \equiv 0 \pmod{p^e} \ \text{ otherwise},$$

unit group is invisible to the power sum.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core arithmetic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def lcm(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Least common multiple of two non-negative integers."""
    if a == 0 or b == 0:
        return 0
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b


def lcm_all(values: Iterable[int]) -> int:
    """Least common multiple of a finite family of positive integers."""
    result = 1
    for v in values:
        result = lcm(result, v)
    return result


def power_sum_mod(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """F_N(k) mod N  =  (1^k + 2^k + ... + N^k) mod N.

    Cost: O(N) modular exponentiations, which is the dominant cost of the
    whole method and the reason it is asymptotically worse than trial
    division.
    """
    total = 0
    for a in range(1, n + 1):
        total += pow(a, k, n)
    return total % n


def power_sum_gcd(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """g_N(k) = gcd(F_N(k), N)."""
    return gcd(power_sum_mod(n, k), n)


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Deterministic trial-division primality test (adequate at these sizes)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Prime factorization of n >= 1 as an exponent dictionary."""
    factors: Dict[int, int] = {}
    m = n
    d = 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            factors[d] = factors.get(d, 0) + 1
            m //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if m > 1:
        factors[m] = factors.get(m, 0) + 1
    return factors


def carmichael_squarefree(n: int) -> int:
    """lambda(N) = lcm over primes p | N of (p-1); valid for squarefree N."""
    return lcm_all(p - 1 for p in factorize(n))

def recover_factors_from_period(n: int, lam: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Recover {p,q} from N and lambda(N), valid when gcd(p-1,q-1) = 1.

    Solves X^2 - sX + N = 0 with s = N + 1 - lambda; returns None if the
    discriminant is not a perfect square (which signals that the guard fails).
    """
    s = n + 1 - lam
    disc = s * s - 4 * n
    if disc < 0:
        return None
    r = isqrt(disc)
    if r * r != disc or (s - r) % 2 != 0:
        return None
    a, b = (s - r) // 2, (s + r) // 2
    if a * b != n or a < 1:
        return None
    return (a, b)

def power_sum_factor(n: int, max_k: Optional[int] = None) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Find a proper factor of N by scanning k = 1, 2, 3, ...

    Returns (k, d) where d is the first proper nontrivial divisor found, or
    None if none is found within the bound.  By the first-hit theorem the
    successful k is min(p-1, q-1) for a semiprime N = pq.
    """
    if max_k is None:
        max_k = isqrt(n) + 1
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        d = power_sum_gcd(n, k)
        if 1 < d < n:
            return (k, d)
    return None


def demo_algorithm() -> None:

    print("=" * 74)
    print("END-TO-END: the reveal algorithm on the test semiprimes")
    print("=" * 74)

    gcd(F_N(k), N) = 1   <=>   lambda(N) | k,   lambda(N) = lcm_{p|N} (p-1).

    gcd(F_N(N-1), N) = 1   <=>   (p-1) | (N-1) for every prime p | N,

Carmichael numbers are precisely the squarefree moduli on which the power-sum
reveal at k = N-1 carries no information whatsoever.

is exponent-specific: for a Carmichael number, exponents that are not multiples
of lambda(N) still leak factors.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List


def factorize(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    f: Dict[int, int] = {}
    m, d = n, 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            f[d] = f.get(d, 0) + 1
            m //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if m > 1:
        f[m] = f.get(m, 0) + 1
    return f


def is_squarefree(n: int) -> bool:
    return all(e == 1 for e in factorize(n).values())


def lam_squarefree(n: int) -> int:
    r = 1
    for p in factorize(n):
        r = r // gcd(r, p - 1) * (p - 1)
    return r


def power_sum_gcd(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    return gcd(sum(pow(a, k, n) for a in range(1, n + 1)) % n, n)


def satisfies_korselt(n: int) -> bool:
    return is_squarefree(n) and all((n - 1) % (p - 1) == 0 for p in factorize(n))

    "algorithm_reveal_scan": """"Power-Sum GCD Factor Revelation — scan exponents until a factor drops out."""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Optional, Tuple


def power_sum_mod(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """F_N(k) mod N = (1^k + 2^k + ... + N^k) mod N.  Cost: O(N log k)."""
    total = 0
    for a in range(1, n + 1):
        total += pow(a, k, n)
    return total % n


def power_sum_gcd(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """g_N(k) = gcd(F_N(k), N)."""
    return gcd(power_sum_mod(n, k), n)


def power_sum_factor(n: int, max_k: Optional[int] = None) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Return (k, d) with d a proper nontrivial divisor of N, found at exponent k.

    For a semiprime N = p*q with p != q the first-hit theorem guarantees that
    the scan succeeds at exactly k = min(p-1, q-1), which satisfies
    (k+1)^2 <= N, so the default bound isqrt(N) always suffices.

    Complexity: O(N) per exponent and O(sqrt N) exponents, hence O(N^{3/2}).
    """
    if n < 4 or n % 2 == 0:
        return (0, 2) if n % 2 == 0 and n > 2 else None
    if max_k is None:
        max_k = isqrt(n) + 1
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        d = power_sum_gcd(n, k)
        if 1 < d < n:
            return (k, d)
    return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for n in (15, 35, 77, 143, 221, 323, 667, 8633):
        print(n, power_sum_factor(n))
",
    "algorithm_period_recovery": """"Carmichael Period Extraction and Vieta Factor Recovery.

Reads the least period lambda(N) off the power-sum gcd sequence as the index of
its first 1, then attempts to recover the factorization.  The recovery step uses
the CORRECT identity

    gcd(p-1, q-1) * lambda(N) + (p + q) = N + 1,

which reduces to the (otherwise false) naive form  p + q = N - lambda(N) + 1
exactly when gcd(p-1, q-1) = 1.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Optional, Tuple


def power_sum_gcd(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    return gcd(sum(pow(a, k, n) for a in range(1, n + 1)) % n, n)


def read_least_period(n: int, max_k: Optional[int] = None) -> Optional[int]:
    """Least k >= 1 with g_N(k) = 1.  Equals lambda(N) for squarefree N.

    Cost: O(N) per exponent, O(lambda(N)) exponents; lambda(N) can be
    Theta(N), so the worst case is O(N^2).
    """
    if max_k is None:
        max_k = n
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        if power_sum_gcd(n, k) == 1:
            return k
    return None


def solve_from_sum_and_product(s: int, n: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Unique ordered pair (a, b), a <= b, with a + b = s and a*b = n; else None.

    Uniqueness is Vieta's: both roots satisfy X(s - X) = n, so any two candidate
    pairs coincide once ordered.
    """
    disc = s * s - 4 * n
    if disc < 0:
        return None
    r = isqrt(disc)
    if r * r != disc or (s - r) % 2:
        return None
    a, b = (s - r) // 2, (s + r) // 2
    return (a, b) if a >= 1 and a * b == n else None


def recover_factors(n: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Factor N by reading its power-sum period, valid when gcd(p-1,q-1) = 1.

    Returns None when the guard fails, which is the honest outcome: without
    gcd(p-1,q-1) the period determines lambda(N) but not phi(N), and hence not
    the factorization.
    """
    lam = read_least_period(n)
    if lam is None:
        return None
    return solve_from_sum_and_product(n + 1 - lam, n)


def corrected_identity_holds(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
    """Verify gcd(p-1,q-1)*lcm(p-1,q-1) + (p+q) = p*q + 1."""
    g = gcd(p - 1, q - 1)
    lam = (p - 1) // g * (q - 1) if g else 0
    return g * lam + (p + q) == p * q + 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for n in (14, 22, 26, 34, 35, 65):
        print(n, "period =", read_least_period(n), "recovered =", recover_factors(n))
    print("identity at (5,13):", corrected_identity_holds(5, 13))

    "algorithm_spectrum_census": """"Master-Formula Spectrum Evaluation and Revealing-Exponent Census.

Given the factorization, the entire power-sum gcd spectrum is computable in O(1)
per exponent, with no summation at all.  This turns an O(N) measurement into a
table lookup and is the tool used to audit the O(N) computation.

It also produces the exact census of revealing exponents inside one Carmichael
period, and the local prime-power correction for non-squarefree moduli.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List


def lcm(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b if a and b else 0


def spectrum_semiprime(p: int, q: int, kmax: int) -> List[int]:
    """g_{pq}(k) for k = 1..kmax, in O(kmax) total time (no power sums)."""
    return [(1 if k % (p - 1) == 0 else p) * (1 if k % (q - 1) == 0 else q)
            for k in range(1, kmax + 1)]


def revealing_exponents(p: int, q: int) -> List[int]:
    """The exponents in (0, lambda] whose gcd is a proper nontrivial divisor."""
    lam = lcm(p - 1, q - 1)
    return [k for k in range(1, lam + 1)
            if ((k % (p - 1) == 0) != (k % (q - 1) == 0))]


def revealing_count_formula(p: int, q: int) -> int:
    """lambda/(p-1) + lambda/(q-1) - 2, the exact census per period."""
    lam = lcm(p - 1, q - 1)
    return lam // (p - 1) + lam // (q - 1) - 2


def local_gcd_prime_power(p: int, e: int, k: int) -> int:
    """gcd(F_N(k), p^e) for an odd prime p with p^e || N.

    Equals p^(e-1) when (p-1) | k and p^e otherwise.  Note the condition is
    (p-1) | k, NOT lambda(p^e) = p^(e-1)(p-1) | k: the p-part of the unit group
    is invisible to the power sum.
    """
    if p == 2:
        raise ValueError("the prime 2 is exceptional and not covered")
    return p ** (e - 1) if k % (p - 1) == 0 else p ** e


def spectrum_general_odd(factorization: Dict[int, int], k: int) -> int:
    """gcd(F_N(k), N) assembled from the local formulas, for odd N.

    Multiplies the local contributions gcd(F_N(k), p^e) over the odd prime
    powers p^e || N.  Valid for k >= 1 and N odd.
    """
    result = 1
    for p, e in factorization.items():
        result *= local_gcd_prime_power(p, e, k)
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(spectrum_semiprime(5, 7, 12))
    print(revealing_exponents(5, 7), revealing_count_formula(5, 7))
    print(spectrum_general_odd({3: 2, 5: 1}, 2))  # N = 45, k = 2  ->  15

over several full periods.  Each exponent k is drawn as a coloured cell:

from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from matplotlib.patches import Patch

    "visualization_barriers": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Visualization: the two quantitative barriers.

Panel A — the first-hit bound.  For every semiprime N = p*q below a cutoff we
plot the first exponent at which the power-sum gcd stops being the trivial
value N,
        k* = min(p-1, q-1),
against N, together with the curve sqrt(N).  The theorem (k*+1)^2 <= N says
every point lies on or below that curve: the reveal always happens before the
square root, and typically only just before.

Panel B — the density of revealing exponents.  Within one Carmichael period
lambda(N) = lcm(p-1,q-1), the number of exponents that expose a proper factor
is exactly
        lambda/(p-1) + lambda/(q-1) - 2 .
We plot the resulting *fraction* of a period that is informative,
        (lambda/(p-1) + lambda/(q-1) - 2) / lambda ,
against N on a log scale.  The fraction decays like 1/sqrt(N): finding a
revealing exponent by blind search is hopeless, which is the quantitative form
of the period-finding barrier.

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def lcm(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b


def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, isqrt(limit) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i:: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i:: i]))
    return [i for i, b in enumerate(sieve) if b]


def semiprime_data(limit: int) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    ps = primes_up_to(int(limit ** 0.5) + 200)
    ns: List[int] = []
    kstars: List[int] = []
    fracs: List[float] = []
    for i, p in enumerate(ps):
        for q in ps[i + 1:]:
            n = p * q
            if n > limit:
                break
            lam = lcm(p - 1, q - 1)
            count = lam // (p - 1) + lam // (q - 1) - 2
            ns.append(n)
            kstars.append(min(p - 1, q - 1))
            fracs.append(count / lam)
    order = np.argsort(ns)
    return (np.array(ns)[order], np.array(kstars)[order], np.array(fracs)[order])


def main() -> None:
    limit = 200_000
    ns, kstars, fracs = semiprime_data(limit)

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.2))

    ax1.scatter(ns, kstars, s=4, alpha=0.35, color="#1f3b73",
                label="k* = min(p−1, q−1)")
    xs = np.linspace(10, limit, 800)
    ax1.plot(xs, np.sqrt(xs), color="#d9453d", lw=2, label=r"$\sqrt{N}$")
    ax1.set_xscale("log")
    ax1.set_yscale("log")
    ax1.set_xlabel("N = pq")
    ax1.set_ylabel("first-hit exponent k*")
    ax1.set_title("A. The first hit always precedes $\\sqrt{N}$\n"
                  "$(k^*+1)^2 \\leq N$", fontsize=11)
    ax1.legend(frameon=False)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")

    ax2.scatter(ns, fracs, s=4, alpha=0.35, color="#0a7f4f",
                label="informative fraction of a period")
    ax2.plot(xs, 2.0 / np.sqrt(xs), color="#d9453d", lw=2,
             label=r"$2/\sqrt{N}$ (reference)")
    ax2.set_xscale("log")
    ax2.set_yscale("log")
    ax2.set_xlabel("N = pq")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"$\left(\frac{\lambda}{p-1}+\frac{\lambda}{q-1}-2\right)/\lambda$")
    ax2.set_title("B. Revealing exponents are vanishingly sparse\n"
                  "the period-finding barrier, quantified", fontsize=11)
    ax2.legend(frameon=False)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")

    fig.suptitle("Why the structure is exact but the algorithm is slow",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("powersum_barriers.png", dpi=160, bbox_inches="tight")
    print("wrote powersum_barriers.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
